title: "Confidence Interval"
description: "A range produced by a procedure designed to cover a population quantity at a specified rate."
term: "Confidence Interval"
letter: "C"
category: "Statistics"
difficulty: "Intermediate"
---

## Simple explanation

A confidence interval gives a range of values produced by a statistical
procedure to express uncertainty about an estimate. A 95% confidence
procedure is designed so that, under its assumptions, intervals from
repeated samples contain the true quantity about 95% of the time.

## Technical explanation

A confidence interval is constructed from data using a method with a
specified long-run coverage property under a model or sampling design.
Its width depends on factors such as sample size, variability, and
confidence level. Different interval methods have different assumptions
and behaviour.

## Why it matters in AI engineering

Metrics estimated on finite data are uncertain. Intervals can help compare
models and communicate how much evidence supports an observed difference,
provided the sampling unit and evaluation design are appropriate.

## How it works

A statistic is calculated from a sample, and a procedure uses the
statistic's sampling variability to form lower and upper bounds. The
interpretation is about the procedure over repeated samples, not a
probability statement about a fixed parameter after observing one
particular interval.

## Practical example

A team estimates a classifier's accuracy on a held-out sample and
calculates an interval. A wide interval signals that the estimate is
uncertain, perhaps because the test set is small.

## Common misconceptions

- A 95% confidence interval does not mean there is a 95% probability that
  the fixed parameter lies in this already-computed interval in the
  frequentist interpretation.
- An interval does not correct a biased or unrepresentative sample.
- Overlapping intervals alone are not a complete test of whether two
  model performances differ.
